job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Felix Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for anything. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at seven because my mum leaves for the care home at half past, and I like the house quiet after that. I'm in my old room in Leicester, so it's mostly job sites, a phone call or two to recruiters, and a long walk to clear my head. In the afternoon I do a bit of unpaid help at my uncle's building firm, carrying and measuring, which at least feels like work.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you study, and what was your final project?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Civil engineering. My final project was a footbridge design over a canal, with load calculations and a cost estimate, and I'm fairly proud of it. I passed without a good grade, because my report was late. I did no placement because the firm I'd lined up closed that summer, and I never found another.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected: noise, and a few small gains. At my uncle's firm they'd shrug, because nobody there trusts a computer to lay a brick. With friends I'd say wait and see, and online I'd stay out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it means the world stays the same, and so does my problem. There aren't many civil jobs near Leicester for juniors, and the ones that exist want a licence or years of site time. I wouldn't expect AI to help me, but it wouldn't hurt me either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying to the same kinds of firms, the councils, the surveyors, the contractors, about eight a week. I'd carry on helping my uncle two or three days, because he's said he might put me on the books in spring. I'd study for the site safety card, which costs a few hundred.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, I suppose, but not at ease. The money is what bothers me. My student loan sits there, and my mum covers the food, which I hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your uncle say about taking you on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He says he'd like to, but the firm only has six people and winter is slow. He told me to ask again in March. I don't want to push him, because he's family and it feels like a favour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your mum covers the food. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not well. She earns a care assistant's wage and works six days some weeks. I try to cook and clean to make up for it, but I know it isn't money. I'd like to hand my mum an envelope at the end of a month, and I'm nowhere near that.

say: I'd say AI is **noise** and a few small gains.
With friends I'd say wait and see; online I'd stay out of it.
think: The world stays the same, and so does my **problem**: few junior civil jobs near Leicester.
AI wouldn't help me but wouldn't hurt me either.
do: Apply to about **eight** councils, surveyors and contractors a week.
Keep helping my uncle's firm and ask again about a place in March.
Pay for the **site safety card**, a few hundred pounds.
feel: Steady but not at ease: the **money** bothers me.
Ashamed that my mum covers my food.
S0.quote: I'd like to hand my mum an envelope at the end of a month, and I'm nowhere near that.
fieldNote: His worry is **money and shame**, not AI; he is also slow to see AI as relevant.
Uncle's firm gives a real route, though a fragile one.
Pragmatic and unhurried; no appetite for risk.

steps.text: Apply to eight councils, surveyors and contractors every week
Ask my uncle again in March about a paid place
Pay for and sit the site safety card course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's fair for desk jobs but I'd like to see it. On a site you still need someone to stand in the mud and check the trench. With friends I'd say let's see who gets hurt, and who gets rich.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think the drawing, calculating and report-writing parts of my degree get taken first. Firms could hire one engineer where they used to hire three juniors. I'd be shut out even more, because drawing and calculating are most of what a graduate does in the first years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lean harder on the site side. Get the safety card, learn to read drawings on the ground, and work for my uncle or any contractor that'll take me. I still wouldn't use AI tools, but I'd probably have to learn what the surveyors use to check things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit more worried than before. It's a slow squeeze, not a bang, so people keep telling me to wait. I don't like waiting when I've no wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd probably have to learn what the surveyors use. What would that mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably drone mapping and the software that turns scans into drawings. I've avoided it because I like doing things the proven way, but the firms near me already use it. If a site foreman showed me, I'd pick it up, though I wouldn't go looking for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mate Callum, who graduated in software the same year. He's applied for ninety jobs and got two interviews. I'm better off than him, because at least I can carry bricks, which is a bleak thing to say.

say: I'd say it's fair for desk jobs but I'd like to **see it**.
On a site you still need someone to check the trench.
think: Drawing, calculating and report writing, my degree's **core tasks**, get taken first.
Firms could hire one engineer where they hired three juniors.
do: Lean harder on **site work** with my uncle or any contractor.
Learn to read drawings on the ground and get the safety card.
Learn the **scanning software** that surveyors use if someone shows me.
feel: A bit more **worried**: a slow squeeze, not a bang.
Impatient, because waiting without a wage is hard.
S1.quote: I'd be shut out even more, because drawing and calculating are most of what a graduate does in the first years.
fieldNote: He separates **desk and site** work clearly and aims at the site.
Still avoids AI tools and would learn them only if shown.
Names a friend, Callum, in software as worse off than him.

steps.text: Work for my uncle or any contractor that will take me on site
Learn to read drawings on a real site
Wait for a foreman to show me the scanning software

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's too fast for anyone to cope with and the government needs to step in. I'd tell my uncle that even he won't be safe in the long run. Online I'd just share what the experts say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it means the design and checking work I trained for disappears first, and the thing left is the site, which robots reach around 2031. So I might have three years of site work if I'm lucky. After that I don't know what's left for a person like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put everything into getting on site now, with my uncle or anywhere else that pays. I'd save every pound I can and try to pay down some of the loan. And I'd talk with my mum about whether we should stay in this house, because if my uncle's firm falls, we'd be in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really sick with it, if I'm honest. I'd be doing sums at night. If it happens that fast, I won't have time to find my feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the three years between the thinking AI and the site robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd be a gap where I earn something. If I'm on a site by 2028 I'd have until 2031 to build savings and maybe move into a supervisor role. That needs a person to be there. After that I'd need to have switched to something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I'd found work on site and I'd handle my own food. I'd also tell her the truth, that I'm scared, because she'd see through me anyway. She'd say we'll get through it, and I'd believe her for about an hour.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** to cope with and the government must step in.
Online I'd share what experts say and nothing more.
think: The design and checking work I trained for **disappears first**.
Site work gives me maybe three years before robots arrive around 2031.
do: Get on a site **now**, with my uncle or anywhere that pays.
Save every pound and pay down some of the loan.
Talk with my mum about whether the **house** is affordable if my uncle's firm fails.
feel: Sick with worry, doing sums at **night**.
Afraid I won't have time to find my feet.
S2.quote: If I'm on a site by 2028 I'd have until 2031 to build savings and maybe move into a supervisor role.
fieldNote: The **three-year gap** before site robots is central to his plan.
His mother's wage and his uncle's small firm are the household's thin supports.
Admits fear to himself more than to others.

steps.text: Get a paid site job within three months
Put every spare pound into paying down the loan
Ask my uncle for steady days through the winter
Plan with my mum whether we can keep the house

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives people a fair chance. I'd tell my uncle to start thinking about what the firm does when software can quote and plan jobs. Online I'd say governments should put money into training now, not later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it gives me time to work my way into the site side and get a licence. By 2031 I could be a few years into a site job and have savings. By 2034 when the robots come, I'd want to be supervising, not carrying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first site job I can get and stay in it, even if the pay is low. I'd do the safety card and a supervisor's course within two years. And I'd keep to my careful ways. I'd save at least a fifth of every wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steadier than the two-year one. It still bothers me that I don't have a job yet, but I can see how to get to 2031 in one piece.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing that would have to go right?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone has to give me a paid start. Everything else follows from that, the course, the savings, the supervising. If that doesn't happen in the first six months, I'm stuck, and I'd need to change my plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you change in the plan if it did not go right?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at moving somewhere with more building work, probably the cities up north, and share a room again. I don't want to leave my mum, but I'd go for a year if there was a job. After that I'd come back, if I could.

say: I'd say five years gives people **a fair chance**.
Online I'd say governments should fund training now, not later.
think: I have time to work into **site work** and get a licence.
By 2034 I want to be supervising, not carrying.
do: Take the first **site job** and stay in it, even at low pay.
Do the safety card and a supervisor's course within two years.
Save at least **a fifth** of every wage.
feel: Still bothered that I have no job, but I can see a **path**.
S3.quote: By 2034 when the robots come, I'd want to be supervising, not carrying.
fieldNote: The longer warning makes his plan stepwise: **start, licence, supervise**.
Everything hangs on someone giving him a paid start in six months.
Would move cities for a year only as a fallback.

steps.text: Take the first paid site job offered
Complete a site supervisor's course within two years
Save a fifth of every wage
Look for building work in northern cities if nothing comes in six months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, so there's no need to run around. I'd tell people to keep working and keep their eyes open. Online, nothing. I just don't see the point in arguing about 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it means I should get on with life. I'd be thirty-three in 2036. In ten years I could be a supervisor or a small contractor, married maybe, with a decent mortgage. AI might change the paperwork, but a person has to run a site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get any paid site job, then work my way up. I'd put some savings aside for a deposit, because I'd rather own a bit of brick than hope for the best. I'd also let my uncle know I'd take over part of the business one day if he's willing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly alright. I'd still have the same money worries now, but they feel less like an emergency. Ten years lets me sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still avoid AI tools over ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not. If everyone around me is using them, I'll learn too, a bit late. I've always been like that. I wait until it's proved, then I do it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be your biggest risk in that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That nothing changes for me for two or three years. If I can't get a first job, ten years shrinks quickly. The time only helps if I get started.

say: I'd say ten years is a long time, so **no need** to run around.
I'd tell people to keep working and keep their eyes open.
think: I should get on with **life**: a supervisor or small contractor by thirty-three.
A person still has to run a site, even if AI changes the paperwork.
do: Get any paid site job, then **work my way up**.
Save for a house deposit rather than hope.
Tell my uncle I'd **take over** part of the firm one day.
feel: Mostly alright, with money worries that no longer feel like an emergency.
S4.quote: I wait until it's proved, then I do it properly.
fieldNote: His **resistance** is a method: wait for proof, then commit.
Long runway turns his worry from emergency to background.
His uncle's firm becomes a long-term plan, not a stopgap.

steps.text: Take any paid site job and work towards supervisor
Wait to adopt AI tools until site foremen use them
Tell my uncle I'd like to take over part of the firm

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd have no time and no savings, and the trade I'm heading for would be next. What would help is a firm that takes me on and trains me, and government that tells people honestly what's coming, not vague promises.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I don't think graduates like me are lazy, whatever people say. I applied to over a hundred jobs and I'm helping at my uncle's firm for free. Give me a start and I'll show up every day.

headlineQuote: I applied to over a hundred jobs and I'm helping at my uncle's firm for free. Give me a start and I'll show up every day.
portrait: **Felix**, 23, graduated in civil engineering without a placement and lives in his old room in Leicester with his mum.
His mum is a care assistant and covers food, and he is ashamed that he can't give her **money**.
Centrist and pragmatic, he avoids risk, never uses AI, and waits for something to be **proven** before changing.
He leans on site work, his uncle's small firm and the three-year gap before robots reach building sites.
His mood is anxious or alarmed until a paid start arrives, and only uneasy in the ten-year world.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world worries him most: no time, no savings and site work next.
He fears being unable to repay his mum's support.
whatWouldHelp: A firm that takes him on and **trains** him, even at low pay.
Government that tells people honestly what is coming.
